growth_story.headline: Income per person in India has grown about 4.5 percent a year since 1990, with no lasting shift through crisis, boom, credit squeeze and pandemic.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990, income per person in India has grown by an average of 4.5 percent a year with no lasting shift. The data show one long era rather than a boom and a bust, and income per person rose from about 538 dollars in 1990 to about 2,523 in 2025 (constant 2015 dollars), its highest level yet. The era opened with the 1991 balance of payments crisis, when income per person fell 1.1 percent; the IMF credits the fiscal and structural reforms that followed with a strong recovery. Investment rose from 26.1 percent of GDP in 1990 to 35.8 percent in 2007, then fell back after the global financial crisis, and IMF researchers found that policy uncertainty and weak business confidence played a key role in that slump. Growth dipped to 2.8 percent in 2019, a slowdown the IMF said weak non-bank lenders made worse, and the COVID-19 lockdown cut income per person by 6.7 percent in 2020 before an 8.8 percent rebound in 2021. From 2022 to 2025, growth stayed between 6.1 and 6.8 percent a year, and the World Bank puts the latest gains down to strong demand at home, helped by low inflation and cuts to income tax and GST.

threads.title: The 1991 crisis and reforms
threads.text: In 1991 India ran short of foreign currency, and income per person fell 1.1 percent. The IMF credits the fiscal and structural reforms that followed for the recovery, and growth in income per person reached 5.4 percent in 1995 and 1996.

citations.title: India at the Crossroads: Sustaining Growth and Reducing Poverty
citations.quote: the broad-ranging fiscal and structural reforms undertaken following the 1991 balance of payments crisis

threads.title: Investment boom, then slump
threads.text: Investment climbed from 26.1 percent of GDP in 1990 to a peak of 35.8 percent in 2007. After the global financial crisis it slid to 28.2 percent in 2016 and 2017. An IMF study found that real interest rates explain only part of the slump, and that uncertainty about policy and weak business confidence played a key role.

citations.title: Disentangling India's Investment Slowdown (Working Paper 14/47)
citations.quote: the results suggest that heightened uncertainty and deteriorating business confidence have played a key role in the recent investment slowdown

threads.text: Growth in income per person fell to 2.8 percent in 2019, and the IMF said weak non-bank lenders made the slowdown in spending worse. The national lockdown in 2020 then cut income per person by 6.7 percent, before an 8.8 percent rebound in 2021.

threads.title: Demand at home carries growth
threads.text: Growth in income per person reached 6.6 percent in 2025, even though the United States raised tariffs on Indian goods. The World Bank points to demand at home, helped by low inflation and cuts to income tax and GST. The IMF expected the GST reform, which lowered the effective tax rate, to help cushion the tariffs.

threads.text: The World Bank reports that a low share of working-age people in India are in the labor force. It notes this in a report on the faster growth India aims for to reach high-income status by 2047.

since_last_year.text: The United States raised tariffs on Indian goods in August 2025, and a GST reform cut the effective tax rate. In February 2026 India moved its GDP figures to a new base year, which lowered the measured size of the economy. The World Bank now expects the conflict in the Middle East to slow growth in the year to March 2027.

growth_story.tension: The sources call India the fastest-growing major economy and describe growth as speeding up. In the data, though, income per person grew 4.9 percent a year over 2016 to 2025, a little slower than the 5.3 percent of 2006 to 2015, because of the 2019 dip and the 2020 fall. The growth rates the sources quote are for total output, which runs ahead of income per person because the population also grew. The February 2026 rebasing also changed the official GDP figures, so the levels in this data may later be revised.
